nameStory: Shingle moss gets its common name from its distinctive growth pattern that resembles overlapping wooden shingles on an old roof. The scientific name 'pennata' means 'feathered' in Latin, referring to the feathery, flat appearance of its branching pattern. It's also called feather flat moss for this same elegant, plume-like quality.
description: Shingle moss is a distinctive flat, feathery moss that grows in elegant, overlapping sheets on tree bark. It forms thin, scale-like patches that lie flat against the surface, creating a shingle-like appearance. The moss has a feathery branching pattern with flattened stems that spread horizontally, typically growing 2-4 inches across in mature patches. Its overall appearance is neat and organized, almost like nature's own green wallpaper.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thin, flat sheets that lie tight against tree bark like overlapping shingles, with a distinctly feathery, organized branching pattern

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny leaves are arranged in neat rows along flattened stems, creating a smooth, almost silky texture when you gently run your finger across them

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green when moist, becoming yellowish-green to brownish when dry, with a subtle glossy sheen that catches light

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels smooth and flat to the touch, almost papery when dry, becoming softer and more pliable when wet

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on the bark of mature sugar maple trees, typically on the north side or in shaded areas of the trunk

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces small, curved capsules on short stalks, but these are relatively uncommon and the moss usually spreads vegetatively

habitat: Shingle moss is found in mature hardwood forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with old sugar maple trees. It prefers the bark of maples that are at least 120 years old, making it an excellent indicator of old-growth or late successional forests. Look for it in shaded, humid forest environments where the air stays moist, often on the north-facing sides of large tree trunks.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as humidity increases, with the feathery pattern most visible as it absorbs spring moisture.
seasonality.summer: Maintains its characteristic flat, shingle-like appearance but may appear more yellowish during dry spells, becoming greener after rain.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most noticeable as deciduous trees lose their leaves, making the moss patches more visible on bare maple trunks.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but appears more brownish and papery, though it quickly greens up when touched by snow melt or winter rains.

funFact: Shingle moss is like a forest detective - finding it tells you you're standing in a forest that's been undisturbed for over a century, since it only grows on sugar maples that are at least 120 years old!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other flat, bark-growing mosses, but shingle moss has the most organized, truly shingle-like pattern. Remember: if it looks like someone carefully arranged tiny green roof shingles on a maple tree, you've found shingle moss.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'feather flat moss' in some guides, it's important not to confuse this with other feather mosses that grow on the ground - shingle moss is specifically a tree-dwelling species that grows only on bark.
compareHints: Since shingle moss is the only Neckera species commonly found in New England, compare it with other flat bark mosses in the broader feather moss group. Shingle moss is distinguished by its more organized, truly shingle-like overlapping pattern and its strong preference for mature maple bark, whereas other flat mosses tend to grow more irregularly and on various tree species.
